newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US presses for improved telecoms deal, EU upbeat.
newsitem.headline: US presses for improved telecoms deal, EU upbeat.

text.p: Negotiators at talks for a global pact to liberalise the $600 billion telecoms trade said on Wednesday a deal was on track ahead of Saturday's deadline.

But U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang said he wanted more improvements in tabled proposals ahead of Saturday, by which time more countries are expected to revise offers listing how far they would open domestic markets to outside competition.
"We're working hard with our negotiating partners to bring this negotiation to a successful conclusion," he said in a brief statement after cancelling a press briefing because of talks.
"We still need to see improvements in the offers on the table."
U.S. negotiators are conducting an assessment of whether they have the "critical mass" of quality offers Washington says it needs to guarantee unfettered foreign access to is market.

Their assessment is vital as the United States is the world's biggest telecoms market and last April derailed a previous talks on a deal, when it walked away arguing that there was not a "critical mass" of good offers on the table.

Trade sources said several countries including Japan remained cautious, but the European Union chief negotiator Karl Falkenberg was upbeat, saying he expected the talks to be successfully completed ahead of Saturday.
"We can relatively confidently say that we look forward to a successful conclusion to the talks by the end of this week," he told reporters.
"I don't expect any difficulties as long as everything that is on the table today is on the table on Saturday. Hopefully we can all go home and even do some skiing on Saturday."
On Wednesday, the EU tabled a final, more liberal proposal and Canada offered to ease controls on domestic satellites.
Falkenberg said the focus had now switched to countries outside the world's four main trading partners -- the United States, the EU, Canada and Japan -- or the so-called "Quad".
The United States and the European Union each represent roughly a third of the global revenue on telecoms markets, followed by Japan with a 15 percent share.

"We have well over 90 percent of the world revenue in telecoms covered by offers of different participants," Falkenberg said. "We certainly think this is an achievement that would make it impossible for members not to conclude the talks."
Some 59 governments representing more than 93 per cent of the global market have submitted offers to open their domestic telecom markets to foreign operators.
A global pact will dramatically cut consumers' telecoms bills, secure a fair playing field and pave the way for mergers in a more competitive industry, Falkenberg said.
One sticking point for Washington was the level of opening to foreign ownership of telecoms companies offered by Canada, which allows a maximum 47.8 percent foreign equity holding.

Senior Canadian trade officials ruled out any change in their stance on Wednesday but instead offered to relax a law requiring the use of Canadian satellites only for domestic satellite communications and to allow foreign operators.
Falkenberg said he expected Washington to be on board,
"They (the U.S.) say more needs to happen, but any good negotiator would say that," he said.
"I think the United States is coming round to a more rational approach (on Canada). I have the impression we are not going to see this issue become a deal-breaker," he said.
"I think the Americans are in a very different mood today than they were in April 1996. I think they have realised the important clarifications and improvements we have achieved."
